lessonTitle: Postmortem Changes, Time Since Death and Patterns of Injury

blocks.text: A gardener is found lying on a greenhouse floor on a cold morning, stiff in the jaw and limbs, with a purple-red discolouration over his back. The police ask the attending doctor one question: how long has he been dead? The honest answer is a range, never a single hour, and this unit shows why. It also teaches you to read wounds and the signs of asphyxia without over-claiming.

blocks.markdown: After death the body changes in a predictable sequence, but the **speed** of each change depends on temperature, clothing, body mass, activity before death and the setting. The changes are therefore used to give a **range**, and the medical opinion must say so. The main early changes are **algor mortis** (cooling), **livor mortis** (postmortem hypostasis or lividity) and **rigor mortis** (postmortem muscle stiffening). Later changes are **putrefaction**, **adipocere** and **mummification**.

blocks.title: Livor mortis, rigor mortis and algor mortis
blocks.text: Livor mortis is the purple-red discolouration of dependent skin caused by gravity pooling blood in vessels after the circulation stops. Rigor mortis is stiffening of skeletal muscle as ATP is depleted and actin-myosin cross-bridges stay locked. Algor mortis is the fall of body temperature towards that of the surroundings.

headers: What it can and cannot tell you
rows: Livor mortis
Becomes visible within about 1 to 2 hours; shifts if the body is turned during the early phase and becomes fixed after several hours
Fixed livor in a non-dependent area suggests the body was moved after it became fixed; pale areas show where pressure from contact surfaces prevented pooling
Rigor mortis
Often starts in small muscles within a few hours, is usually fully developed by around 12 hours, and passes over 1 to 2 days; much faster in heat or after violent exertion
Cannot give a precise time; heat and exertion before death accelerate it, cold slows it
Algor mortis
Cooling over many hours, usually with an initial plateau
Depends on ambient temperature, clothing, body mass and air movement; wide error range
Putrefaction
Visible changes such as greenish discolouration of the abdominal wall and then marbling over days, faster in heat
Depends strongly on temperature and moisture; not a precise clock
Adipocere
Weeks to months in moist, anaerobic conditions
Indicates a prolonged interval and a wet environment, not a date
blocks.caption: Postmortem changes. All timings are approximate and vary widely; check current forensic references.

blocks.markdown: **Estimating time since death.** A single method is never reliable. Experts combine temperature, rigor, livor, putrefaction, stomach contents (poor reliability), vitreous humour potassium (limited, with wide error) and the scene circumstances (last known alive, mail, phone, food). The **Henssge nomogram** is a method that uses rectal and ambient temperature, body weight and correction factors to give a time estimate with a wide confidence interval. It is validated only under certain conditions and the interval can be several hours. A simple **rule of thumb** states that a body in a moderate environment cools by about 1.5 degrees Fahrenheit (about 0.8 degrees Celsius) per hour after an initial plateau. It is a teaching approximation, not a measurement.

blocks.caption: Rough estimate of hours since death, with T in the same units as the cooling rate (for example 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit and 1.5 degrees per hour). Real error is several hours.

blocks.title: Applying the rough cooling rule
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old man is found in an indoor storeroom with a rectal temperature of 86.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Assume a pre-death body temperature of 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit and a cooling rate of 1.5 degrees per hour, as a crude teaching estimate.

steps.text: Compute the temperature fall: 98.6 minus 86.6 equals 12.0 degrees Fahrenheit.
Divide by the assumed rate: 12.0 divided by 1.5 equals 8.0 hours.

State the result as a range, not a point: roughly 8 hours, but the true interval could easily be several hours either side because clothing, room temperature, body mass and pre-death fever or exertion alter cooling.
Cross-check against rigor and livor. If rigor is passing off and livor is fixed, the estimate must be weighed against them, and the circumstances (last seen alive) used to narrow the window.

blocks.answer: About 8 hours by the rough rule, offered only as an approximate range and combined with other findings.

blocks.markdown: **Wound classification.** A forensic description uses the type of force and the wound's morphology. An **abrasion** is damage to the epidermis by friction or impact, often showing a pattern. A **contusion** (bruise) is bleeding into the tissue from ruptured small vessels with the skin surface intact; its colour cannot reliably date it. A **laceration** is a tear of skin and deeper tissue from blunt force, with irregular, often abraded margins and tissue bridges across the wound. An **incised wound** is made by a sharp edge and is longer on the skin than it is deep, with clean edges and no tissue bridging. A **stab wound** is deeper than it is long on the skin surface and is made by a pointed object.

rows: Abrasion
Friction or impact scrapes the epidermis
Superficial, may show pattern, no full-thickness loss
Contusion
Blunt force ruptures small vessels
Discolouration with intact skin; colour not a reliable age
Laceration
Blunt force tears or splits tissue
Irregular, abraded margins, tissue bridging, bruising nearby
Incised wound
Sharp edge drawn across skin
Longer than deep, clean-cut margins, no bridging, may gape
Stab wound
Pointed object driven in
Deeper than long on the skin surface; track depth matters; edges reflect blade shape
blocks.caption: Common wound types.

blocks.title: Classifying two wounds
blocks.prompt: Wound A on the forearm is 2.0 cm long on the skin and its track is 9 cm deep. Wound B on the scalp is 3 cm long with irregular abraded edges and strands of tissue crossing the wound.

steps.text: For wound A, compare surface length (2.0 cm) with depth (9 cm). Depth exceeds length, so it is a stab wound by definition.
For wound B, note the irregular, abraded edges and tissue bridging. These point to blunt tearing over bone, not a sharp edge, so it is a laceration despite looking linear.
State what the classification supports: type of force and weapon characteristics, not the identity of the weapon or the person responsible.
Record measurements, site and description in a body diagram so another expert can review them.

blocks.answer: Wound A is a stab wound; wound B is a laceration caused by blunt force.

blocks.markdown: **Firearm injuries.** The skin wound often helps distinguish **entrance** from **exit**. An entrance wound typically has a rim of **marginal abrasion** (an abrasion collar) where the projectile scrapes through skin. At close range, hot gases and unburnt powder may cause soot deposition, singeing and **tattooing (stippling)**; contact wounds may show a muzzle imprint and gaping from gas expansion. Exit wounds tend to be irregular or stellate, without an abrasion collar, though supported skin can mimic abrasion. Range estimates depend on the weapon and ammunition and are given tentatively.

blocks.title: Do not over-interpret
blocks.text: Wound morphology suggests mechanism and approximate range, but cannot identify the perpetrator. Describe what you see, measure it, avoid terms such as 'defence wound' unless the pattern and the circumstances justify it, and distinguish what is observation from what is opinion.

blocks.markdown: **Asphyxia, hanging and drowning.** Asphyxia means failure of oxygen delivery to tissues. General signs (congestion, cyanosis, **petechiae** in the face and conjunctivae) are non-specific. In **hanging**, the ligature mark is typically oblique, placed high on the neck above the thyroid cartilage, often with a gap where the knot lifts the ligature (an inverted V). In **ligature strangulation**, the mark is usually horizontal, lower on the neck and encircling it. **Manual strangulation** may show fingertip bruises and fractures of the hyoid or laryngeal cartilages. **Drowning** is largely a diagnosis of exclusion: froth at the mouth and nostrils and waterlogged lungs are suggestive but not conclusive, and tests such as diatom analysis have limited reliability.

rows: Typical ligature or neck mark
Oblique, high, often incomplete with a gap at the suspension point
Horizontal, often lower, encircling
None unless coincidental
Petechiae
Variable, often fewer when the weight is fully suspended
More common and prominent
Non-specific
Laryngeal fractures
Less frequent
More frequent in manual strangulation than in hanging
Not typical
Diagnosis
Scene, mark and exclusion of other causes
Scene, mark and exclusion of other causes
Largely by exclusion with scene and circumstance
blocks.caption: Comparing asphyxial deaths. Findings overlap; circumstances are essential.

points: Postmortem changes give a range for time since death, not a single time; temperature, rigor, livor and putrefaction all depend on conditions.
Temperature formulae and the Henssge nomogram are rough estimates with wide error ranges and must be combined with circumstantial evidence.
Wounds are classified by morphology: abrasion, contusion, laceration, incised, stab and firearm, each suggesting a mechanism but never identifying a person.
Hanging, ligature strangulation and drowning show overlapping features, so the pathologist integrates scene, neck findings and exclusion of other causes.

questions.stem: A woman is found lying supine. Her body shows fixed purple-red discolouration across the front of her chest and abdomen, with blanched areas where she lay on the floor boards. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: She died lying face down and was later turned onto her back after the livor had become fixed
Livor mortis has not yet begun
She died of drowning
Rigor mortis has already passed

questions.correctOptionText: She died lying face down and was later turned onto her back after the livor had become fixed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fixed livor on the anterior surface in a body found supine suggests she was moved after livor was fixed.
distractorRationale.b: The discolouration is described as fixed, so livor is present.
distractorRationale.c: Livor pattern does not identify the cause of death.
distractorRationale.d: The stem gives nothing about rigor.

questions.explanation: Livor mortis is gravitational and becomes fixed after several hours. Fixed livor on a non-dependent surface suggests the body lay in another position and was moved. It does not by itself show how the person died.

questions.stem: A man is found dead in a cool room with a rectal temperature of 80.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Using the teaching approximation that body temperature before death was 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit and that the body cools at 1.5 degrees Fahrenheit per hour, estimate the time since death in hours. This is a rough estimate with wide error.
questions.explanation: The temperature fall is 98.6 minus 80.6, which is 18.0 degrees Fahrenheit. Dividing by 1.5 degrees per hour gives 12.0 hours. This is only a crude teaching estimate and the real interval is uncertain by several hours.

questions.stem: Rigor mortis timing can be used to state the exact hour of death.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Rigor onset and resolution vary with temperature, muscle mass and activity before death, so it gives only a rough range. Estimates must be combined with other findings and the circumstances.

questions.stem: Which factor would be expected to slow the cooling of a body after death?

options.text: A thin body in a cold, windy outdoor setting
Heavy insulating clothing and high body fat in a warm room
Immersion in cold water
Removal of clothes

questions.correctOptionText: Heavy insulating clothing and high body fat in a warm room

distractorRationale.a: Thin body and wind accelerate heat loss.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: insulation and fat retain heat and slow cooling.

questions.explanation: Heat loss depends on insulation, surface area to mass ratio and environment. Insulating clothing and subcutaneous fat slow cooling, which is why temperature-based estimates carry wide error ranges.

questions.stem: A round wound on the chest is surrounded by a thin rim of circumferential abrasion, with no soot, singeing or tattooing in the surrounding skin. Which is the most appropriate description?

options.text: Exit wound from a close-range shotgun
Entrance wound, with no features of close-range discharge
Incised wound
Postmortem artefact only

questions.correctOptionText: Entrance wound, with no features of close-range discharge

distractorRationale.a: Exit wounds typically lack an abrasion collar and are irregular.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: an abrasion collar suggests entrance, and absence of soot or tattooing suggests more than close range.
distractorRationale.c: Incised wounds are linear, with clean margins.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the stem suggests a postmortem artefact.

questions.explanation: An entrance wound usually shows marginal abrasion where the projectile scrapes the skin. The absence of soot, singeing and tattooing suggests the muzzle was not close, but range estimates are tentative and depend on the weapon.

questions.stem: An area of bluish-purple discolouration with intact skin develops after a blow from a blunt object. This is best classified as:

options.text: Contusion
Laceration
Incised wound
Stab wound

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bleeding into tissue with an intact surface is a contusion.
distractorRationale.b: A laceration is a tear of the skin.
distractorRationale.c: An incised wound has a cut skin surface.
distractorRationale.d: A stab wound is deeper than long and breaks the skin.

questions.explanation: A contusion is extravasation of blood into tissue from ruptured vessels, leaving the epidermis intact. Its colour is a poor guide to age, so dating should be avoided or hedged.

questions.stem: A 3 cm skin wound on the forehead has clean edges and no tissue bridges. A second 4 cm wound on the scalp has irregular edges and tissue bridges. Explain how you would classify each wound, why it matters, and the limits of your inference.
markingGuide: Identifies the first wound as incised (sharp edge, clean margins) and the second as a laceration (blunt tearing)
States that incised wounds are longer on the skin than deep, while lacerations show bridging and abraded margins
Explains that classification suggests the type of force, not the identity of a weapon or person
Mentions measurement and body diagram documentation
Notes that scalp wounds over bone can split like a cut, so classification needs careful examination
questions.explanation: Morphology reveals the mechanism, but scalp lacerations can look sharp. Careful inspection for bridging and margin abrasion prevents mislabelling and misleading opinions.

questions.stem: Which neck finding most favours hanging rather than ligature strangulation?

options.text: A horizontal mark encircling the whole neck at the level of the lower neck
An oblique mark rising towards a gap above the thyroid cartilage
Fingertip bruising on both sides of the neck
Multiple fractures of the laryngeal cartilages from manual compression

questions.correctOptionText: An oblique mark rising towards a gap above the thyroid cartilage

distractorRationale.a: This is more typical of ligature strangulation.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: an oblique, high mark with a gap at the suspension point favours hanging.
distractorRationale.d: Laryngeal fractures are more typical of manual strangulation.

questions.explanation: In hanging the ligature is pulled upwards by the body weight, so the mark is oblique and often incomplete. Ligature strangulation tends to produce a horizontal, lower mark. Findings overlap, so the scene remains essential.

questions.stem: Which statement about the diagnosis of drowning is correct?

options.text: Diatoms in the lungs prove drowning in every case
Drowning is largely a diagnosis of exclusion that relies on circumstances and exclusion of other causes
Petechiae are pathognomonic for drowning
Froth at the nose and mouth is always present and always diagnostic

questions.correctOptionText: Drowning is largely a diagnosis of exclusion that relies on circumstances and exclusion of other causes

distractorRationale.b: Correct: no single finding is conclusive, so the diagnosis rests on scene, findings and exclusion of other causes.
distractorRationale.c: Petechiae occur in many asphyxial deaths.
distractorRationale.d: Froth is suggestive, not constant or conclusive.

questions.explanation: No autopsy sign is pathognomonic for drowning. The pathologist integrates the scene, the body findings and exclusion of other causes, and states uncertainty openly.

questions.stem: A body is found hanging from a beam. Describe the findings that would help a pathologist distinguish hanging from ligature strangulation, and explain why the scene is also needed.
markingGuide: Hanging: oblique mark, high on the neck above the thyroid cartilage, often incomplete with a gap at the suspension point
Ligature strangulation: horizontal, lower, encircling mark
Petechiae and laryngeal fractures vary and overlap between the two
Scene findings, ligature, knot, position and circumstances must be integrated
Findings can overlap, so conclusions are given with appropriate uncertainty
questions.explanation: Neck findings suggest mechanism but overlap. A secure conclusion integrates the scene, ligature, body findings and history.
